questions.stem: Chlorthiazide and furosemide are members of different diuretic classes, in terms of mechanisms of action, but they share the ability to cause hypokalemia. Which of the following statements best describes the general mechanism by which these drugs cause their effects that lead to net renal loss of potassium?

options.label: B
options.text: Inhibiting Na+-K+-2C1– cotransport in the ascending limb of loop of Henle

options.label: C
options.text: Increasing the availability of Na+ in the distal tubular fluid to exchange with interstitial K+

questions.answerText: Increasing the availability of Na+ in the distal tubular fluid to exchange with interstitial K+
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C. Increasing the availability of Na+ in the distal tubular fluid to exchange with interstitial K+.

 

Both chlorthiazide and furosemide act by inhibiting sodium reabsorption at different parts of the nephron. Chlorthiazide acts at the distal convoluted tubule, while furosemide acts at the ascending limb of the Loop of Henle. As a result, they both increase the concentration of sodium in the distal tubular fluid. This increased sodium is then available for exchange with potassium, leading to enhanced potassium excretion and thereby increasing the risk of hypokalemia.

 

Option A. inhibiting proximal tubular K+ reabsorption: Neither chlorthiazide nor furosemide act primarily on the proximal tubule to inhibit potassium reabsorption.

 

Option B. Inhibiting Na+-K+-2Cl– cotransport in the ascending limb of loop of Henle: While it is true that furosemide works at this site, the mechanism of action does not directly involve potassium loss. Chlorthiazide does not act at this site at all.

 

Option D. Potentiating the action of aldosterone: Neither chlorthiazide nor furosemide potentiate the action of aldosterone. They can indirectly cause an increase in aldosterone due to volume depletion but do not potentiate its action directly.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old man is scheduled for emergency surgery due to acute appendicitis. He has no significant past medical history, but his medical team is concerned about the use of succinylcholine as a neuromuscular blocking agent for intubation. Which of the following statements about succinylcholine is true?

options.label: B
options.text: It has a long duration of action.

options.label: C
options.text: It is the drug of choice in non-traumatic rhabdomyolysis.

options.label: D
options.text: It is useful in patients with spinal cord injuries with paraplegia.

questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A. It may induce life-threatening hyperkalemia.

 

Succinylcholine is a depolarizing neuromuscular blocker that can potentially induce life-threatening hyperkalemia, especially in patients with pre-existing hyperkalemia, burns, or certain neuromuscular disorders. This risk is a critical consideration when choosing a neuromuscular blocker for intubation or surgery.

 

Other options:

 

Option B. It has a long duration of action: Succinylcholine has a very short duration of action, usually lasting only a few minutes. This makes it ideal for short procedures but contradicts this statement.

 

Option C. It is the drug of choice in non-traumatic rhabdomyolysis: Succinylcholine is contraindicated in cases of rhabdomyolysis, as it may exacerbate hyperkalemia and worsen the condition.

 

Option D. It is useful in patients with spinal cord injuries with paraplegia: Succinylcholine is generally avoided in patients with spinal cord injuries due to the risk of hyperkalemia.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old woman presents with acute liver and renal failure. Her lab reports show a serum bilirubin level of 8 mg/dl and a serum creatinine level of 4 mg/dl. She requires muscle relaxation for mechanical ventilation. What would be the muscle relaxant of choice in this patient?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C. Atracurium.

 

Atracurium is metabolized through Hoffman elimination, which is independent of hepatic and renal function. Therefore, it is a suitable choice for patients with liver and kidney dysfunction.

 

Other options:

 

Option A. Pancuronium: This muscle relaxant undergoes hepatic metabolism and renal excretion, making it less suitable for patients with liver and kidney dysfunction.

 

Option B. Mivacurium: Mivacurium is metabolized by plasma cholinesterase and undergoes renal excretion. Liver disease can result in decreased cholinesterase activity, which would prolong the duration of action of mivacurium.

 

Option D. d-Tubocurarine: This muscle relaxant is primarily excreted by the kidneys, and thus is not suitable for patients with renal failure.



ore, it is a suitable choice for patients with liver and kidney dysfunction.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old woman presents to the clinic with a 3-month history of a persistent cough, unintentional weight loss, and night sweats. A chest X-ray reveals findings consistent with pulmonary tuberculosis. After confirming the diagnosis, the physician prescribes a multi-drug therapy (MDT) regimen. What is the most important reason for using MDT in her treatment?

options.label: A
options.text: To enhance the speed of clinical recovery

options.label: B
options.text: To reduce the duration of treatment

options.label: C
options.text: To prevent the emergence of drug-resistant strains

options.label: D
options.text: To reduce the adverse side effects of anti-tubercular drugs

questions.answerText: To prevent the emergence of drug-resistant strains
questions.solutionHtml:
n>

A. To enhance the speed of clinical recovery

While MDT can help in effective treatment and clinical recovery, this is not the primary reason for its use. The main goal is to prevent drug resistance.

B. To reduce the duration of treatment

Although MDT can help to reduce the overall duration of treatment compared to monotherapy, this is not the primary reason for its use. The main objective remains the prevention of drug-resistant TB strains.

D. To reduce the adverse side effects of anti-tubercular drugs

Each anti-tubercular drug can have side effects. By using multiple drugs, it's possible to give each drug at a lower dose than if used alone, potentially reducing the severity of side effects. However, this is not the primary reason for using MDT. The main rationale behind MDT is the prevention of drug resistance, not the minimization of side effects.

Educational Objective

Multi-drug therapy (MDT) is crucial in the treatment of tuberculosis to prevent the emergence of drug-resistant strains of Mycobacterium tuberculosis. While MDT can also reduce the overall treatment duration, its primary purpose is to ensure that the bacteria are effectively eradicated by using a combination of drugs, thereby minimizing the risk of developing resistance to any single drug.

questions.stem: A 27-year-old male diagnosed with HIV seeks guidance from his primary care doctor for appropriate treatment. Given the significant drop in his CD4 counts, initiation of HAART (Highly Active Antiretroviral Therapy) is being contemplated. Concerning the role of ritonavir for this patient, which statement holds true?

options.label: A
options.text: Ritonavir is commonly used to inhibit the HIV protease enzyme along with other drugs in HAART regimen.

options.label: B
options.text: This agent is associated with resistance when used in combination with another protease inhibitor.

options.label: C
options.text: It is used primarily for its inhibitory effect on CYP3A4.

options.label: D
options.text: This is an excellent single agent for use in HAART therapy.

questions.answerText: It is used primarily for its inhibitory effect on CYP3A4.
questions.solutionHtml:
/span>

A. Ritonavir is commonly used to inhibit the HIV protease enzyme along with other drugs in HAART regimen.

While ritonavir does have protease inhibitory activity, its primary role in HAART regimens is as a pharmacokinetic enhancer of other protease inhibitors rather than as the main protease inhibitor.

B. This agent is associated with resistance when used in combination with another protease inhibitor.

Ritonavir, when used in low doses as a booster, does not contribute significantly to resistance. Its role is to increase the effectiveness of other protease inhibitors without leading to increased resistance.

D. This is an excellent single agent for use in HAART therapy.

Ritonavir is not used as a single agent in HAART therapy due to its side effect profile and the development of resistance when used alone. It is always used in combination with other antiretroviral drugs.

Educational Objective

Ritonavir is primarily used in HAART regimens for its strong inhibitory effect on the cytochrome P450 enzyme CYP3A4. This inhibition enhances the pharmacokinetics of other protease inhibitors, increasing their plasma levels and efficacy, which allows for lower dosages and reduced side effects.

questions.stem: A 31-year-old female discovered she was HIV-positive four weeks ago. Upon receiving her diagnosis, she initiated a HAART (Highly Active Antiretroviral Therapy) protocol. Currently, she's experiencing symptoms of nausea, episodes of vomiting, and stomach pain. Lab tests indicate a heightened serum amylase level. If these symptoms are a result of her medication, which antiretroviral drug is most likely the culprit?
questions.solutionHtml:
strong>

A. Efavirenz

Efavirenz is a non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor (NNRTI) that is more commonly associated with central nervous system side effects such as dizziness, insomnia, and vivid dreams rather than gastrointestinal side effects and pancreatitis.

C. Raltegravir

Raltegravir is an integrase strand transfer inhibitor (INSTI) and is not typically associated with pancreatitis. Its common side effects include elevated creatine kinase, muscle pain, and insomnia.

D. Nevirapine

Nevirapine is another NNRTI that is primarily associated with hepatotoxicity and skin rash, including severe reactions like Stevens-Johnson syndrome, rather than pancreatitis.

Educational Objective

Didanosine, an NRTI used in HAART regimens, is associated with gastrointestinal side effects, including pancreatitis. Elevated serum amylase levels, along with symptoms such as nausea, vomiting, and stomach pain, are indicative of pancreatitis.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old sexually active, HIV-negative male visits his healthcare provider with a painless sore on his inner lip and a non-itchy rash on the soles of his feet. He recalls having a non-tender ulcer on his scrotum about a month and a half ago, which resolved on its own. He receives an intramuscular injection of benzathine penicillin G and is discharged. How might the treatment approach for this patient have been modified?

options.label: A
options.text: The choice of antibiotic was not appropriate, and another class should have been selected.

options.label: B
options.text: The correct treatment would involve a different form of penicillin G, rather than benzathine.

options.label: C
options.text: There is no need for changes; the treatment administered is correct.

options.label: D
options.text: After the initial injection, a follow-up dose should be given after 7 days.

questions.answerText: There is no need for changes; the treatment administered is correct.
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C. There is no need for changes; the treatment administered is correct.

 

The patient's clinical presentation, including a painless sore followed by a rash on the soles of the feet, is consistent with secondary syphilis.

  • The first-line treatment for syphilis at any stage is penicillin, specifically benzathine penicillin G, which is long-acting and given intramuscularly. Thus, another antibiotic class isn't needed.

  • Benzathine penicillin G is the appropriate form of penicillin for the treatment of syphilis. It is the recommended preparation due to its prolonged action which provides a sustained therapeutic level for an extended period.

  • The single intramuscular injection of benzathine penicillin G is the appropriate treatment for early syphilis, which includes both primary and secondary stages.

  • A single dose of benzathine penicillin G is sufficient for the treatment of primary or secondary syphilis in HIV-negative individuals. The follow-up dose after 7 days is recommended for the late latent stage or tertiary syphilis, but not for early syphilis.

questions.stem: A 25-year-old man presents to the emergency room with seizures. A CT scan of his head reveals a space-occupying lesion, suggesting a diagnosis of neurocysticercosis. Which of the following medications is not recommended for treating this patient's condition?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B. Di-Ethyl-Carbamezine

 

  • Carbamazepine:
    Carbamazepine is an anticonvulsant medication commonly used to control seizures. Given that the patient presented with seizures, this drug would be an appropriate choice for symptom management.

  • Di-Ethyl-Carbamezine:
    Di-Ethyl-Carbamezine is not typically used for treating neurocysticercosis or seizures associated with it. In fact, it is used for the treatment of filariasis and is not recommended for neurocysticercosis.

  • Albendazole:
    Albendazole is an antiparasitic medication that is commonly used for treating neurocysticercosis. It kills the cysticercus, the larval form of the Taenia solium tapeworm that causes the condition.

  • Prednisolone:
    Prednisolone is a corticosteroid that may be used to reduce inflammation and edema around the cysts in the brain, especially during the initial phase of anthelmintic therapy, to avoid inflammatory responses as the parasites die.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old woman presents to the clinic for a routine check-up. Blood tests reveal elevated liver enzymes, and subsequent tests confirm a diagnosis of chronic hepatitis C. She has no significant medical history and wishes to begin antiviral therapy to minimize the risk of progression to liver cirrhosis or hepatocellular carcinoma. Which of the following oral medications is recommended as a first-line treatment for hepatitis C?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C. Sofosbuvir

 

  • Ribavirin:
    Ribavirin is an older antiviral medication that was used in combination with interferon for treating hepatitis C. It is not commonly used as a monotherapy for hepatitis C and has largely been replaced by more effective and tolerable options.
  • Tenofovir:
    Tenofovir is primarily used in the treatment of HIV and chronic hepatitis B, not hepatitis C.
  • Sofosbuvir:
    Sofosbuvir is a first-line, direct-acting antiviral agent used for the treatment of chronic hepatitis C. It is often used in combination with other medications and has a high cure rate with a well-tolerated side effect profile.
  • Lamivudine:
    Lamivudine is used for the treatment of hepatitis B and HIV but is not effective for treating hepatitis C.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old male patient presents to the hospital with a 6-week history of progressive dyspnea, fatigue, and a productive cough with greenish sputum. He has a past medical history of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) and has been treated multiple times for respiratory infections, though he mentions that they were never this prolonged or severe. On physical examination, you notice decreased breath sounds and crackles in the right lower lobe. A sputum culture identifies Pseudomonas aeruginosa. Which of the following antimicrobial agents is not effective against this organism?
questions.solutionHtml:
ns. B. Vancomycin

 

Explanation:

 

Pseudomonas aeruginosa is a gram-negative bacterium, and as such, it is inherently resistant to many antibiotics including vancomycin.

 

Among the options provided:

  • Rifampicin can have activity against a variety of pathogens including gram positive bacteria like MRSA and gram negative bacteria like Pseudomonas.

  • Vancomycin is primarily effective against gram-positive organisms and lacks efficacy against Pseudomonas aeruginosa.

  • Ceftazidime, a third-generation cephalosporin, has good activity against Pseudomonas aeruginosa.

  • Ciprofloxacin, a member of the fluoroquinolones, is effective against Pseudomonas aeruginosa.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old patient presents to the clinic with a swollen, painful abscess on the forehead that is discharging pus. The clinical findings strongly suggest a pus-forming gram-positive bacterial infection. Which of the following antibiotics is least likely to be effective for treating this infection?
questions.solutionHtml:

Explanation:

  4. Cephalexin: A first-generation cephalosporin that effectively targets gram-positive cocci and is often employed for skin and soft tissue infections.

questions.stem: true statement regarding vancomycin is:

options.label: B
options.text: It has the advantage of high oral bioavailability

options.label: C
options.text: Staphylococcal enterocolits occurs commonly with its use

options.label: D
options.text: It is not susceptible to penicillinases

questions.answerText: It is not susceptible to penicillinases
questions.solutionHtml:
ible to penicillinases

 

Explanation:

  1. It is bacteriostatic: Vancomycin is primarily bactericidal. This means it actively kills bacteria rather than merely inhibiting their growth.

  2. It has the advantage of high oral bioavailability: Vancomycin has poor oral bioavailability. When given orally, it doesn't absorb well from the gastrointestinal tract, so its oral form is mainly used to treat C. difficile colitis. For systemic infections, it's typically given intravenously.

  3. Staphylococcal enterocolitis occurs commonly with its use: Staphylococcal enterocolitis isn't a common association with vancomycin use. However, antibiotics, including vancomycin, can be associated with antibiotic-induced diarrhea or colitis, most famously caused by Clostridium difficile.

  4. It is not susceptible to penicillinases: This is true. Vancomycin's action is distinct from beta-lactams. It binds to the D-Ala-D-Ala terminus of the cell wall precursor units, preventing cell wall synthesis. As a result, penicillinases, which break down the beta-lactam ring in penicillins, don't affect vancomycin.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old male with a history of chronic kidney disease is being considered for treatment with a broad-spectrum antibiotic. The clinician is considering imipenem. Which of the following statements about imipenem is most accurate?

options.label: A
options.text: The drug has a narrow spectrum of antibacterial action

options.label: B
options.text: It is used in fixed dose combination with sulbactum

options.label: C
options.text: In renal dysfunction, dosage reductions are necessary to avoid seizures

options.label: D
options.text: Imipenem is active against methicillin-resistant staphylococci

questions.answerText: In renal dysfunction, dosage reductions are necessary to avoid seizures
questions.solutionHtml:
to avoid seizures

 

Explanation:

  1. The drug has a narrow spectrum of antibacterial action: Imipenem is a broad-spectrum carbapenem antibiotic effective against both gram-positive and gram-negative bacteria, including many that are resistant to other antibiotics.
  2. It is used in fixed dose combination with sulbactum: Imipenem is commonly combined with cilastatin, not sulbactum. Cilastatin inhibits the renal enzyme that metabolizes imipenem, thereby prolonging its action.
  3. In renal dysfunction, dosage reductions are necessary to avoid seizures: This statement is accurate. Imipenem, when used in high doses or in patients with renal dysfunction, can lead to neurotoxic effects, including seizures. Thus, dose adjustments are required in patients with kidney impairment to minimize this risk.
  4. Imipenem is active against methicillin-resistant staphylococci: While imipenem has a broad spectrum of activity, most strains of methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) are resistant to it.

questions.stemHtml: Chemical structure of a drug is shown in the figure below. It is drug of choice for:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B. Scrub typhus

 

The given structure corresponds to ‘tetracycline’ group of drugs as suggested by four cycles in the structure.

  • For Enteric fever, antibiotics like ceftriaxone or azithromycin are typically used.
  • Scrub typhus is best treated with doxycycline, which belongs to the tetracycline class of antibiotics.
  • MRSA (Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus) is commonly treated with drugs like vancomycin. Some tetracyclines might be active against certain strains but are not the first-line choice.
  • Gonorrhea is primarily treated with ceftriaxone and azithromycin, not tetracyclines.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements is true about pseudomembranous colitis?

options.label: A
options.text: Intravenous vancomycin can be used as an alternative in patients not responding to fidaxomicin

options.label: B
options.text: Bezlotoxumab is a highly effective monoclonal antibody that can kill most of Clostridium difficile bacteria responsible for the infection

options.label: C
options.text: Clostridium difficile is the common organism implicated in the causation of Pseudomembranous colitis

questions.answerText: Clostridium difficile is the common organism implicated in the causation of Pseudomembranous colitis
questions.solutionHtml:
licated in the causation of Pseudomembranous colitis

 

Explanation:

  • Intravenous vancomycin is not typically used for pseudomembranous colitis. Instead, oral vancomycin is used because it achieves high concentrations in the colon, where the infection is located. Intravenous administration doesn't reach effective concentrations in the colon. Now, the drug of choice for pseudomembranous colitis is fidaxomicin.
  • Bezlotoxumab is a monoclonal antibody against toxin B of Clostridium difficile. While it can reduce the recurrence of Clostridium difficile infection (CDI) in patients who are at high risk for CDI recurrence, it does not "kill" the bacteria. Instead, it neutralizes one of the toxins produced by the bacteria.
  • Clostridium difficile is indeed the common organism implicated in the causation of Pseudomembranous colitis. The disease arises from the toxin production of this bacterium, typically after antibiotic therapy has disrupted the normal gut flora.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old male presents to his primary care physician with complaints of a persistent sore throat, fever, and swollen glands for the past week. On examination, the physician observes inflamed tonsils with a white exudate. The doctor is considering using a cephalosporin. She is debating which generation to use and recalls a drug she learned about during her medical training. Which of the following cephalosporins, that the doctor is considering, is a second-generation cephalosporin?
questions.solutionHtml:
an>

 

Explanation:

 

  • Cefprozil is a second-generation cephalosporin. These are often used for respiratory tract infections.

  • Cefadroxil is a first-generation cephalosporin.

  • Ceftizoxime is a third-generation cephalosporin.

  • Ceftobiprole is a fifth-generation cephalosporin.

questions.stemHtml: Which of the following drugs reversibly binds the site labelled as B in the given figure?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Ticagrelor

 

  • The figure shows a platelet activation and aggregation pathway involving the COX-1 enzyme, thromboxane, ADP, the P2Y12 receptor, and the GPIIb/IIIa receptor. 
  • The site labelled "B" is the P2Y12 receptor, which is targeted by antiplatelet drugs.
  • Ticagrelor is unique because it reversibly binds to the P2Y12 receptor.
  • Thus, the drug that reversibly binds the site labelled "B" (P2Y12 receptor) is ticagrelor.
  • Site A: The site labelled "A" in the figure corresponds to the COX-1 enzyme. COX-1 is responsible for the production of thromboxane A2, a potent promoter of platelet aggregation. The primary drug that targets this site is aspirin, which irreversibly inhibits COX-1, leading to a decrease in thromboxane A2 production and thus reduced platelet aggregation.
  • Site C: The site labelled "C" in the figure corresponds to the GPIIb/IIIa receptor. This receptor is crucial for platelet aggregation because it binds fibrinogen, which links platelets together. Drugs that target this receptor, known as GPIIb/IIIa inhibitors, include abciximab, eptifibatide, and tirofiban. These drugs prevent fibrinogen binding to the GPIIb/IIIa receptor, thereby inhibiting platelet aggregation.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. B and D. Clopidogrel, Prasugrel, and Ticlopidine: Irreversibly bind to the P2Y12 receptor to inhibit ADP-induced platelet aggregation.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • Understanding the mechanisms of action of antiplatelet drugs is crucial for their effective use in preventing thrombotic events. 
  • Ticagrelor is a reversible P2Y12 receptor antagonist, which distinguishes it from other P2Y12 inhibitors like clopidogrel, prasugrel, and ticlopidine, which bind irreversibly. 
  • Aspirin targets the COX-1 enzyme, reducing thromboxane A2 production, while GPIIb/IIIa inhibitors prevent platelet aggregation by blocking fibrinogen binding.

questions.stem: A 56-year-old chronic alcoholic man is brought to the emergency department due to an altered mental status. Blood tests show normal creatinine levels but indicate hyperammonemia. After administering lactulose, his blood ammonia levels soon drop to a more appropriate range. Which organ is the primary site of action for lactulose?
questions.solutionHtml:
ion of Other Options

A. Brain

While the effects of hyperammonemia are seen in the brain, lactulose does not act directly on the brain to lower ammonia levels.

C. Kidney

The kidneys are not the primary site of action for lactulose. Lactulose primarily acts in the colon to decrease blood ammonia levels indirectly.

D. Liver

Although the liver is the organ responsible for metabolizing ammonia, lactulose does not act directly on the liver. It reduces ammonia absorption in the colon, thereby indirectly lowering the ammonia load that the liver needs to detoxify.

Educational Objective

Lactulose is used to treat hyperammonemia, particularly in hepatic encephalopathy, by acting in the colon. It is metabolized by colonic bacteria to lower the pH, converting ammonia to ammonium, which is less absorbable and thus reduces blood ammonia levels.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements about warfarin group of oral anticoagulants is false?

options.label: A
options.text: They interfere with an early step in the synthesis of clotting factors

options.label: B
options.text: Irrespective of the dose administered, their anticoagulant effect has a latency of onset of 4-5 days

options.label: C
options.text: Their dose is adjusted by repeated measurement of INR

options.label: D
options.text: They are contraindicated during first trimester of pregnancy

questions.answerText: They interfere with an early step in the synthesis of clotting factors
questions.solutionHtml:
trong>

 

B. Irrespective of the dose administered, their anticoagulant effect has a latency of onset of 4-5 days

 

This statement is true. Warfarin has a delayed onset of action because it does not affect clotting factors that have already been synthesized and are present in the bloodstream. It takes several days for these existing clotting factors to degrade and for the anticoagulant effect to become apparent.

 

C. Their dose is adjusted by repeated measurement of INR

 

This statement is true. The dose of warfarin is adjusted based on the International Normalized Ratio (INR) to ensure that the patient's blood is maintained within the therapeutic range, which minimizes the risk of bleeding and thromboembolism.

 

D. They are contraindicated during first trimester of pregnancy

 

This statement is true. Warfarin is contraindicated during pregnancy, especially in the first trimester, due to its teratogenic effects. It can cause fetal warfarin syndrome, characterized by nasal hypoplasia and stippled epiphyses, among other congenital abnormalities.

 

Educational Objective

 

Warfarin is an oral anticoagulant that inhibits the enzyme vitamin K epoxide reductase, affecting the carboxylation and activation of certain clotting factors. It has a delayed onset of action, typically taking 4-5 days, and its dose is adjusted based on INR measurements. Warfarin is contraindicated during pregnancy due to its teratogenic potential, especially in the first trimester.

questions.stem: An old woman is required to receive 4 cycles of cancer chemotherapy. After her first cycle, she developed chemotherapy induced thrombocytopenia. Then in the next cycle, it would be appropriate to give this patient:
questions.solutionHtml:
t-family:"Times New Roman",serif">Darbepoetin alpha is an erythropoiesis-stimulating agent used to treat anemia, particularly in patients with chronic kidney disease or chemotherapy-induced anemia. It is not effective for treating thrombocytopenia.

B. Filgrastim

Filgrastim (G-CSF) is used to stimulate the production of white blood cells and is effective for preventing and treating chemotherapy-induced neutropenia. It does not address thrombocytopenia.

C. Iron dextran

Iron dextran is used to treat iron deficiency anemia. It does not affect platelet counts and is not used to manage chemotherapy-induced thrombocytopenia.

Educational Objective

In cases of chemotherapy-induced thrombocytopenia, the appropriate treatment is to use a thrombopoietic agent such as oprelvekin (interleukin-11) to stimulate platelet production.

questions.stem: Which antiemetic drug selectively blocks levodopa induced vomiting without blocking its anti-Parkinsonian action?
questions.solutionHtml:
span style="font-family:"Times New Roman",serif">Explanation of Other Options:

A. Metoclopramide

Metoclopramide is a dopamine antagonist that crosses the blood-brain barrier and can block dopamine receptors both peripherally and centrally. While it can be effective in controlling nausea and vomiting, it can also interfere with the anti-Parkinsonian effects of levodopa by blocking central dopamine receptors, potentially worsening Parkinson's symptoms.

B. Cisapride

Cisapride is a prokinetic agent that enhances gastrointestinal motility by increasing the release of acetylcholine at the myenteric plexus. It is not specifically used to block levodopa-induced vomiting and does not have a selective dopamine antagonist effect at the CTZ.

D. Ondansetron

Ondansetron is a selective serotonin 5-HT3 receptor antagonist used primarily to prevent nausea and vomiting caused by chemotherapy, radiation therapy, and surgery. It does not have the specific action needed to selectively block levodopa-induced vomiting without affecting its anti-Parkinsonian action.

Educational Objective:

Domperidone selectively blocks levodopa-induced vomiting without interfering with its anti-Parkinsonian action, making it the preferred antiemetic for patients with Parkinson's disease experiencing nausea and vomiting from levodopa therapy. Other antiemetics, such as metoclopramide, can block central dopamine receptors and potentially worsen Parkinson's symptoms

questions.stem: A 40-year-old woman, Seema was a resident of Nubra Valley in Leh Ladakh. She underwent a kidney transplant at AIIMS, Delhi. After transplant she was started several immunosuppressant drugs, including daily prednisone. She had returned to her home at Nubra Valley and is taking prednisone for the past two months since her transplant. However, she is trapped in her house due to heavy snow and may soon run out of prednisone. What health risk is she most likely to face if she does not get her prednisone in time?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C. Cardiovascular collapse

  • If a patient suddenly stops taking prednisone after being on it for more than a few weeks, they may not have enough cortisol in their system to respond to stress. This can lead to a serious condition called HPA axis suppression resulting in adrenal crisis or acute adrenal insufficiency, which can manifest as severe fatigue, weakness, nausea, vomiting, low blood pressure, and potentially cardiovascular collapse if not treated. This is why it's important to gradually taper the dose of prednisone, rather than stopping it abruptly.
  • While long-term use of corticosteroids can increase the risk of osteoporosis (option A) and cause sleep disturbances (option D), these are not the immediate risks of abruptly stopping prednisone. These are rather potential long-term side effects of the medication.
  • Increased risk of infections (option B) occurs due to overuse of steroids and is not a complication of sudden stoppage of steroids.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old individual named Suresh, who has been diagnosed with insulin-dependent diabetes mellitus, has been prescribed insulin therapy. The discomfort from the injections has become unbearable for him, leading him to attempt consuming the insulin orally from the vial that was initially intended for subcutaneous injection. What is the most likely consequence of his action?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C. Chronic high blood sugar levels

  • Insulin is a hormone that helps regulate blood glucose levels. It is typically administered through injection because it is a peptide and would be broken down in the digestive system if taken orally, rendering it ineffective. So, if Suresh drinks his insulin instead of injecting it, it will not have the intended effect of lowering his blood glucose levels. This will result in persistent hyperglycemia (high blood sugar levels), which can lead to a variety of health problems if left untreated, including damage to the eyes, kidneys, and nerves, heart disease, stroke, and even diabetic coma.
  • As for the other options, while gastrointestinal upset (A), vomiting (B), and kidney failure (D) can occur in diabetes, they are not the direct result of drinking insulin. These conditions can be related to complications from uncontrolled diabetes or its treatment, but they are not the immediate result of the route of administration of insulin being changed from injection to oral consumption.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements about dapagliflozin is true?

options.label: A
options.text: Its major mode of action in diabetes mellitus is to cause glucosuria when serum glucose is above 180 mg/dL.

options.label: B
options.text: It acts by inhibiting SGLT2 present in collecting tubules of the nephron

options.label: C
options.text: Urinary tract infections are common with its use

questions.answerText: Urinary tract infections are common with its use
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C. Urinary tract infections are common with its use

 

Let us analyse each option one by one:

 

Option A. Its major mode of action in diabetes mellitus is to cause glucosuria when serum glucose is above 180 mg/dL: This statement is not correct. Dapagliflozin, an SGLT2 inhibitor, reduces blood glucose levels by blocking glucose reabsorption in the kidneys, leading to increased glucose excretion in the urine (glucosuria). This effect occurs regardless of whether the blood glucose level is above or below 180 mg/dL. The traditional concept of a renal threshold for glucose around 180 mg/dL applies to normal physiology without SGLT2 inhibition. SGLT2 inhibitors lower this threshold, causing glucosuria even at lower blood glucose levels.

 

Option B. It acts by inhibiting SGLT2 present in the collecting tubules of the nephron: This statement is incorrect. Though dapagliflozin inhibits SGLT2 but it is primarily located in the proximal convoluted tubule, not in the collecting tubules.

 

Option C. Urinary tract infections are common with its use: This is true. The use of SGLT2 inhibitors like dapagliflozin is associated with an increased risk of urinary tract infections due to the presence of higher glucose levels in the urine, which can foster bacterial growth.

 

Given this information, the true statement about dapagliflozin is option c: "Urinary tract infections are common with its use."

questions.stem: Which of the following statements about elagolix is false?

options.label: A
options.text: It is a gonadotropin release hormone antagonist

options.label: C
options.text: It is approved for treatment of pain due to endometriosis

options.label: D
options.text: It can cause hot flashes as adverse effect

questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) It is not effective orally

 

  • Elagolix is an orally active gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) antagonist. 
  • It is effective when taken by mouth, which makes it a convenient option for patients. 
  • This statement is false because elagolix is indeed effective when administered orally.

 

Other Options: 

 

Option A. It is a gonadotropin release hormone antagonist: This statement is true. Elagolix works as a GnRH antagonist, which means it inhibits the action of GnRH and reduces the production of gonadotropins (LH and FSH).

 

Option C. It is approved for treatment of pain due to endometriosis: This statement is true. Elagolix has been approved by the FDA for the treatment of moderate to severe pain associated with endometriosis.

 

Option D. It can cause hot flashes as adverse effect: This statement is true. One of the known adverse effects of elagolix is the occurrence of hot flashes, which is related to its mechanism of reducing estrogen levels in the body.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • Elagolix is an orally active gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) antagonist approved for the treatment of moderate to severe pain associated with endometriosis. 
  • It effectively reduces the production of gonadotropins and estrogen, which can alleviate endometriosis-related pain. 
  • However, its estrogen-lowering effect can lead to side effects such as hot flashes. 
  • Understanding the pharmacokinetics, therapeutic indications, and potential adverse effects of elagolix is crucial for its appropriate use in clinical practice.

questions.stem: Which of the following drug can decrease bone resorption as well as increase bone formation?
questions.solutionHtml:
Explanation of Other Options

 

A. Denosumab

 

Denosumab is a monoclonal antibody that inhibits RANKL (receptor activator of nuclear factor kappa-Β ligand), leading to decreased bone resorption. It does not significantly increase bone formation. Denosumab is used primarily to prevent bone loss in conditions like osteoporosis and certain cancers.

 

C. Teriparatide

 

Teriparatide is a recombinant form of parathyroid hormone (PTH) that primarily stimulates bone formation. It is used to treat osteoporosis by increasing bone formation but does not significantly decrease bone resorption. Teriparatide is typically reserved for patients with severe osteoporosis or those who have not responded to other treatments.

 

D. Cinacalcet

 

Cinacalcet is a calcimimetic agent used to treat secondary hyperparathyroidism in patients with chronic kidney disease and hypercalcemia in patients with parathyroid carcinoma. It lowers parathyroid hormone (PTH) levels by increasing the sensitivity of calcium-sensing receptors in the parathyroid gland. Cinacalcet does not directly affect bone resorption or formation.

 

Educational Objective

 

Romosozumab uniquely decreases bone resorption and increases bone formation by inhibiting sclerostin. In contrast, denosumab decreases bone resorption by inhibiting RANKL, teriparatide increases bone formation as a recombinant PTH, and cinacalcet lowers PTH levels without directly affecting bone metabolism.

questions.stem: Raj Kumar, a 50-year-old patient with schizophrenia, has been stable on clozapine therapy for the last 3 years. His regular blood tests have been satisfactory and his plasma clozapine level remains within the therapeutic range. He has no other major health issues. Which of the following statements about clozapine is incorrect?

options.label: A
options.text: Clozapine is considered a last resort antipsychotic due to its risk of severe side effects.

options.label: B
options.text: Regular monitoring of total leucocyte count is recommended while patient is on clozapine therapy.

options.label: C
options.text: The risk of agranulocytosis with clozapine is significantly high if plasma concentration exceeds 600 ng/mL.

options.label: D
options.text: Clozapine is associated with an increased risk of cardiovascular disease.

questions.answerText: The risk of agranulocytosis with clozapine is significantly high if plasma concentration exceeds 600 ng/mL.
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C. The risk of agranulocytosis with clozapine is significantly high if plasma concentration exceeds 600 ng/mL.

 

To identify the incorrect statement about clozapine, let's examine each option:

 

Option A. Clozapine is considered a last resort antipsychotic due to its risk of severe side effects: This statement is correct. Clozapine is often considered a treatment of last resort for schizophrenia, primarily used when patients do not respond to other antipsychotic medications. Its use is restricted because of serious side effects, including agranulocytosis (a potentially life-threatening reduction in white blood cells).

 

Option B. Regular monitoring of total leukocyte count is recommended while patient is on clozapine therapy: This statement is correct. One of the most serious side effects of clozapine is agranulocytosis, so regular monitoring of the total leukocyte count (especially neutrophils) is crucial to detect this condition early.

 

Option C. The risk of agranulocytosis with clozapine is significantly high if plasma concentration exceeds 600 ng/mL: This statement is misleading. While higher plasma levels of clozapine are associated with an increased risk of adverse effects, there is no specific threshold level at which the risk of agranulocytosis becomes 'significantly high.' As agranulocytosis is dose independent adverse effect of clozapine. The risk of agranulocytosis is more closely related to the duration of therapy, particularly the first few months, rather than the plasma concentration of the drug.

 

Option d. Clozapine is associated with an increased risk of cardiovascular disease: This statement is correct. Clozapine has been associated with an increased risk of metabolic syndrome, which includes weight gain, dyslipidemia, and diabetes, all of which are risk factors for cardiovascular disease. Additionally, clozapine can cause myocarditis and cardiomyopathy.

 

Given these considerations, the incorrect statement about clozapine is option c: "The risk of agranulocytosis with clozapine is significantly high if plasma concentration exceeds 600 ng/mL."

 

Educational Objective

Clozapine is an atypical antipsychotic reserved for treatment-resistant schizophrenia due to its risk of severe side effects, including agranulocytosis. Regular monitoring of total leukocyte count is essential to detect potential agranulocytosis early. However, the risk of agranulocytosis is dose independent. Clozapine is also associated with an increased risk of cardiovascular disease, requiring careful monitoring of patients for cardiovascular health.

questions.stem: A large number of deaths of drug abusers were reported who had purchased and self-administered illicit drugs that contained lethal amounts of fentanyl. One patient who received this fentanyl-laced drug presents in your emergency department, barely alive. Which of the following drugs should you administer first, with the best hope that it can promptly reverse the lethal effects of the fentanyl?
questions.solutionHtml:
n:justify">B. Diazepam

Diazepam is a benzodiazepine used primarily for its anxiolytic, muscle relaxant, and anticonvulsant properties. It does not counteract the effects of opioids like fentanyl and is not suitable for reversing opioid overdose.

C. Flumazenil

Flumazenil is a benzodiazepine antagonist used to reverse the effects of benzodiazepines. It has no effect on opioid receptors and therefore cannot reverse the effects of fentanyl.

D. Fomepizole

Fomepizole is an antidote for methanol and ethylene glycol poisoning. It inhibits the enzyme alcohol dehydrogenase, preventing the formation of toxic metabolites. It does not interact with opioid receptors and is not useful in treating opioid overdose.

Educational Objective

In cases of opioid overdose, particularly with potent opioids like fentanyl, the first line of treatment is the administration of naloxone. Naloxone is an opioid antagonist that effectively and rapidly reverses the life-threatening effects of opioid overdose, including respiratory depression and sedation. Other drugs such as diazepam, flumazenil, and fomepizole are not effective in treating opioid overdose, as they do not target opioid receptors.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements about vigabatrin is false ?

options.label: A
options.text: It acts by inhibiting the enzyme GABA transaminase

options.label: B
options.text: It is utilized for treatment of infantile spasms

options.label: C
options.text: It can cause visual field contraction as an adverse effect.

options.label: D
options.text: It is a competitive antagonist of GABA-A receptors

questions.answerText: It is a competitive antagonist of GABA-A receptors
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) It is a competitive antagonist of GABA-A receptors

 

It is a competitive antagonist of GABA-A receptors: This statement is false. Vigabatrin does not act as a competitive antagonist at GABA-A receptors. Instead, as mentioned in option a, its primary mechanism of action is the inhibition of GABA transaminase, leading to increased GABA levels.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. It acts by inhibiting the enzyme GABA transaminase: This statement is true. Vigabatrin works by irreversibly inhibiting GABA transaminase, the enzyme responsible for the breakdown of GABA (gamma-aminobutyric acid). This inhibition increases the levels of GABA, an inhibitory neurotransmitter in the brain, which contributes to its anticonvulsant effects.

 

Option B. It is utilized for treatment of infantile spasms: This statement is true. Vigabatrin is used in the treatment of infantile spasms (West syndrome), particularly when they are associated with tuberous sclerosis. It's also used for the treatment of refractory complex partial seizures.

 

Option C. It can cause visual field contraction as an adverse effect: This statement is true. One of the significant adverse effects of vigabatrin is the risk of causing permanent visual field defects (particularly peripheral visual field contraction). Due to this risk, regular ophthalmological monitoring is recommended for patients on vigabatrin.

Vigabatrin is an anticonvulsant that acts by inhibiting the enzyme GABA transaminase, thereby increasing the levels of GABA in the brain. questions.stem: All of the following are adverse effects associated with haloperidol except:
questions.solutionHtml:
-size:16px;">Explanation of Other Options

 

A. Akathisia

 

Akathisia is a common adverse effect of haloperidol. It is characterized by a feeling of inner restlessness and an inability to stay still, often due to the drug's D2 receptor blockade in the basal ganglia.

 

B. Hyperprolactinemia

 

Hyperprolactinemia is another adverse effect of haloperidol. This occurs because haloperidol blocks D2 receptors in the pituitary gland, leading to increased secretion of prolactin.

 

D. Hypotension

 

Hypotension, particularly orthostatic hypotension, can occur with haloperidol use. This is due to its alpha-adrenergic blocking properties, which cause vasodilation and a subsequent drop in blood pressure.

 

Educational Objective

 

Haloperidol, a typical antipsychotic, can cause various adverse effects such as akathisia, hyperprolactinemia, and hypotension due to its pharmacological actions, including D2 receptor blockade. However, its D2 blocking action in the chemoreceptor trigger zone (CTZ) also provides antiemetic properties, making vomiting an unlikely adverse effect.

questions.stem: A patient Komal having depressive disorder has taken 25 times the normal dose of amitriptyline. Which of the following is not likely to be observed in this patient?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Pinpoint pupil

 

Amitriptyline is a tricyclic antidepressant (TCA). In overdose, TCAs cause severe anticholinergic toxicity, sodium channel blockade in the heart, and CNS effects.

 

Key toxic effects:

 

  • Cardiac: Arrhythmias, prolonged QRS, hypotension (due to α-blockade and myocardial depression).
  • Anticholinergic: Hot dry skin, hyperthermia, mydriasis (dilated pupils), urinary retention.
  • CNS: Delirium, seizures, coma.

 

Pinpoint pupils are characteristic of opioid overdose, not TCA poisoning. In fact, TCAs cause dilated pupils due to anticholinergic effect.

Other Options:

 

Option A. Arrhythmias: Likely. Due to sodium channel blockade, conduction delay, ventricular tachyarrhythmias are common and life-threatening.

 

Option B. Hot dry skin: Likely. Due to strong antimuscarinic effects, sweating is reduced → skin becomes dry, warm, and flushed.

 

Option D. Hypotension: Likely. Due to α1-adrenergic blockade and myocardial depression.

questions.stem: The combination of alcohol and disulfiram results in nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain and hypotension as a result of accumulation of:
questions.solutionHtml:
Acetate is the product of the metabolism of acetaldehyde by aldehyde dehydrogenase. Since disulfiram inhibits this enzyme, acetate does not accumulate.

B. Methanol

Methanol is a different type of alcohol and is not related to the metabolic pathway of ethanol or the effects of disulfiram.

D. NADH

NADH is a coenzyme involved in various metabolic processes, including alcohol metabolism, but its accumulation is not the primary cause of the disulfiram-alcohol reaction symptoms.

Educational Objective

The combination of alcohol and disulfiram leads to the accumulation of acetaldehyde due to the inhibition of aldehyde dehydrogenase. This accumulation causes adverse reactions like nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, and hypotension, which are meant to deter alcohol consumption.

The rats were tested with tail flick test, a model to test analgesic effect of drugs. After giving all opioids, there is increase in duration in tail flick test signifying the analgesic effect. questions.stem: A 38-year-old woman was started on esketamine therapy. Which of the following clinical scenarios best represents its unique therapeutic use?

options.label: A
options.text: Immediate relief of anxiety in generalized anxiety disorder

options.label: B
options.text: Rapid reduction of suicidal ideation in major depressive disorder

options.label: C
options.text: Long-term prevention of manic episodes in bipolar disorder

options.label: D
options.text: Improvement of obsessive-compulsive symptoms within 24 hours

questions.answerText: Rapid reduction of suicidal ideation in major depressive disorder
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Rapid reduction of suicidal ideation in major depressive disorder

 

Esketamine’s unique advantage over SSRIs, SNRIs, and MAOIs is its rapid antidepressant effect within hours, particularly helpful in acute suicidal risk.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Immediate relief of anxiety in generalized anxiety disorder: Incorrect. Benzodiazepines provide rapid anxiolysis, not esketamine.

 

Option C. Long-term prevention of manic episodes in bipolar disorder: Incorrect. Mood stabilizers (lithium, valproate) prevent mania, not esketamine.

 

Option D. Improvement of obsessive-compulsive symptoms within 24 hours: Incorrect. SSRIs and CBT are mainstay for OCD. Esketamine is not indicated.

questions.stem: This drug is approved for treatment of angina pectoris as well as for CHF. Its primary action is to decrease heart rate without affecting the AV nodal conduction or ventricular contractility. It may produce adverse effects on the vision. Which drug is being discussed about?
questions.solutionHtml:
style="color:#000000">Explanation of Other Options:

Option B: Levosimendan 

Levosimendan enhances cardiac contractility by sensitizing troponin C to calcium and opening ATP-sensitive potassium channels. It is primarily used for acute decompensated heart failure. Although it can cause hypotension and arrhythmias, it does not lead to significant visual disturbances, distinguishing it from ivabradine.

Option C: Omapatrilat 

Omapatrilat inhibits both angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) and neutral endopeptidase (NEP). It was investigated for heart failure and hypertension but is not widely approved due to safety concerns, particularly the risk of angioedema. Unlike ivabradine, omapatrilat does not cause visual disturbances.

Option D: ARNI (Angiotensin Receptor-Neprilysin Inhibitor) 

ARNI, such as sacubitril/valsartan, combines neprilysin inhibition with angiotensin II receptor blockade, promoting vasodilation, natriuresis, and inhibition of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system. It is approved for heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF). Common adverse effects of ARNI include hypotension, hyperkalemia, and renal impairment, but visual disturbances are not a typical side effect.

Educational Objective: 

Ivabradine is used to treat angina and heart failure by decreasing heart rate through selective inhibition of the If current in the sinoatrial node, without affecting AV nodal conduction or ventricular contractility. It can cause visual disturbances as a notable side effect.

questions.solutionHtml:
Roman",serif">Explanation of Other Options:

Option A: Quinidine 

Quinidine is a class IA antiarrhythmic drug that not only prolongs the action potential but also has effects on sodium channels, leading to a decrease in the slope of phase 0 (depolarization) of the action potential.

Option B: Amiodarone 

Amiodarone is a class III antiarrhythmic drug that prolongs the action potential duration but also has multiple effects on sodium, potassium, and calcium channels, as well as adrenergic receptors, making its action more complex and not purely limited to action potential prolongation.

Option D: Lignocaine

Lignocaine (also known as Lidocaine) is a class IB antiarrhythmic drug that primarily shortens the action potential duration and has effects on sodium channels, leading to a decrease in the slope of phase 0 (depolarization) of the action potential.

 

Educational Objective: 

Ibutilide is a pure action potential prolonging drug, primarily affecting potassium channels without other significant effects on the action potential, unlike other antiarrhythmics like amiodarone, lignocaine and quinidine, which have multiple channel effects.

options.label: C
options.text: Has no hypolipidemic action, but combined with niacin

options.label: D
options.text: MTP inhibitor used to decrease VLDL

questions.answerText: Has no hypolipidemic action, but combined with niacin
questions.solutionHtml:
an>

Option A: A bile acid sequestrant 

Bile acid sequestrants are a class of drugs that bind bile acids in the intestine, preventing their reabsorption and thereby lowering cholesterol levels. Examples include cholestyramine, colestipol, and colesevelam. Laropiprant is not a bile acid sequestrant.

Option B: A cholesterol absorption inhibitor 

Cholesterol absorption inhibitors, such as ezetimibe, work by preventing the absorption of cholesterol from the intestine, leading to lower blood cholesterol levels. Laropiprant is not a cholesterol absorption inhibitor.

Option D: MTP inhibitor used to decrease VLDL 

MTP (microsomal triglyceride transfer protein) inhibitors, like lomitapide, are used to decrease very-low-density lipoprotein (VLDL) and LDL cholesterol levels by inhibiting the assembly and secretion of lipoproteins. Laropiprant is not an MTP inhibitor.

Educational Objective: 

Laropiprant is used in combination with niacin to reduce niacin-induced flushing, improving the tolerability of niacin therapy, which is effective in managing dyslipidemia. It does not have hypolipidemic action on its own.

She previously developed severe muscle pains on both atorvastatin and rosuvastatin. Her physician prescribes bempedoic acid. Which of the following is most accurate regarding this drug?

This reduces hepatic cholesterol synthesis, increases LDL receptor expression, and lowers LDL-C. This mechanism is independent of HMG-CoA reductase, explaining its use in statin-intolerant patients.

questions.stem: Atropine is useful in organophosphate poisoning because it:

options.label: C
options.text: Binds with both nicotinic and muscarinic acetylcholine receptors

options.label: D
options.text: Is a competitive antagonist of acetylcholine

questions.answerText: Is a competitive antagonist of acetylcholine
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Is a competitive antagonist of acetylcholine

 

  • Atropine is useful in organophosphate poisoning because it acts as a competitive antagonist of acetylcholine at muscarinic receptors.
  • Organophosphates inhibit acetylcholinesterase, the enzyme responsible for breaking down acetylcholine in the synaptic cleft. 
  • This leads to an excessive accumulation of acetylcholine, which overstimulates the muscarinic receptors throughout the body.
  • Atropine, as a competitive antagonist, binds to the muscarinic receptors and blocks the action of acetylcholine. 
  • By doing so, atropine helps to counteract the excessive stimulation of muscarinic receptors caused by the organophosphate poisoning. 
  • This can alleviate symptoms such as excessive salivation, bronchoconstriction, bradycardia, and gastrointestinal distress that result from excessive cholinergic activity.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Reactivates acetylcholine esterase: This statement is incorrect. Atropine does not reactivate acetylcholinesterase. Instead, it acts as a competitive antagonist of acetylcholine at muscarinic receptors, blocking the excessive stimulation caused by the inhibition of acetylcholinesterase. Oximes act by reactivating acetylcholine esterase.

 

Option B. Competes with acetylcholine release: This statement is also incorrect. Atropine does not compete with acetylcholine release. It acts on the postsynaptic receptors (muscarinic receptors) rather than affecting the release of acetylcholine.

 

Option C. Binds with both nicotinic and muscarinic acetylcholine receptors: This statement is also incorrect. While atropine primarily binds to muscarinic receptors, it has minimal affinity for nicotinic receptors. Its main action is on muscarinic receptors, blocking the effects of acetylcholine at these receptors.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • Atropine is a competitive antagonist of acetylcholine at muscarinic receptors and is used in organophosphate poisoning to reverse muscarinic symptoms. 
  • Pralidoxime is required to reactivate acetylcholinesterase and relieve nicotinic effects.

questions.stem: During your rural posting after the internship, you encounter a patient of acute cardiac failure. Your preferred drug for this condition is dobutamine. However, it is not available there. Which of the following other drugs, or combination of drugs, would be a suitable alternative, giving the pharmacologic equivalent of what you want the dobutamine to do?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A. Norepinephrine plus phentolamine

Dobutamine primarily stimulates beta-1 adrenergic receptors leading to increased myocardial contractility (positive inotropy) and slightly increased heart rate (positive chronotropy) with minimal effects on blood vessels (vasculature).

Among the options given:

a. Norepinephrine plus Phentolamine - Norepinephrine stimulates alpha 1, alpha 2 and beta 1 receptors whereas Phentolamine is a nonselective alpha-adrenergic antagonist that would block both alpha 1 and alpha 2 receptors. So, the net effect is stimulation of beta 1 receptors only. This combination thus produces the action similar to dobutamine.

b. Dopamine (at a very high dose) - Dopamine at high doses stimulates alpha-1, beta-1, and dopaminergic receptors. While the beta-1 effect may be beneficial similar to dobutamine, the alpha-1 adrenergic stimulation could increase afterload and thus is not an ideal substitute for dobutamine.

c. Ephedrine plus Propranolol - Ephedrine is a non-selective adrenergic agonist stimulating both alpha and beta receptors. Propranolol is a non-selective beta-adrenergic antagonist. This combination result in stimulation of only alpha receptors and thus is not an ideal replacement for dobutamine.

Atropine blocks the parasympathetic stimulation of the heart leading to an increase in heart rate but doesn't have a significant inotropic effect. Thus this combination cannot be used as a replacement of dobutamine.

questions.stem: All of the following are features of atenolol in comparison to propranolol EXCEPT?

options.label: A
options.text: It is ineffective in suppressing muscle tremor

options.label: C
options.text: It is less likely to cause bradycardia

options.label: D
options.text: It is less likely to worsen Raynaud’s disease

questions.answerText: It is less likely to cause bradycardia
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C. It is less likely to cause bradycardia

  • Atenolol and propranolol are both beta-blockers, but they have different selectivities. Atenolol is a selective beta-1 blocker, meaning it primarily affects beta-1 adrenergic receptors found mostly in the heart. Propranolol is a non-selective beta-blocker and blocks both beta-1 and beta-2 adrenergic receptors, the latter of which are found in the lungs, blood vessels, and skeletal muscles.
  • Considering the options:
    • It is ineffective in suppressing muscle tremor: This is true. Propranolol can suppress muscle tremors because it blocks beta-2 adrenergic receptors found in the muscles. Atenolol, being a beta-1 selective blocker, does not have this effect.
    • It is safer in asthmatics: This is also true. Beta-2 adrenergic receptor blockade can lead to bronchoconstriction, which can be dangerous in patients with asthma. Because atenolol selectively blocks beta-1 receptors, it is safer for asthmatics than propranolol.
    • It is less likely to cause bradycardia: This statement is false. Both atenolol and propranolol, by virtue of blocking beta-1 adrenergic receptors in the heart, can cause bradycardia (slowing of the heart rate). Atenolol is not less likely to cause bradycardia compared to propranolol.
    • It is less likely to worsen Raynaud’s disease: True. Propranolol can exacerbate Raynaud's disease, a condition characterized by decreased blood flow to the extremities in response to cold or stress, due to its non-selective blockade of beta receptors, including those causing vasoconstriction in the skin (beta-2). Atenolol, with its selective beta-1 activity, is less likely to have this effect.
  • So, the statement that does not hold true when comparing atenolol with propranolol is option c i.e. It is less likely to cause bradycardia.

questions.stemHtml: The effect of different drugs was tested on heart rate. Curve A represents the effect of adrenaline (a pure beta 1 re ceptor agonist). Which of the curves most likely represents the effect of adrenaline after application of a reversible competitive beta 1 receptor antagonist?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans.  D. E

 

The image shows a dose-response curve with several different curves representing the biological effect of various drugs at increasing log drug concentrations. Typically, when a reversible competitive antagonist is applied to a system where an agonist like adrenaline is acting, the effect of the antagonist is to shift the dose-response curve of the agonist to the right without changing the maximal response. This is because a competitive antagonist competes with the agonist for the same binding site on the receptor.

 

Given that curve A represents the effect of adrenaline (a pure beta-1 receptor agonist), we would expect the curve representing the effect of adrenaline after the application of a reversible competitive beta-1 receptor antagonist to:

 

  1. Have the same maximal efficacy because the antagonist is competitive (reversible), meaning it can be overcome by a high enough concentration of the agonist.

  2. Require a higher concentration of adrenaline to achieve the same levels of biological effect, because the presence of the antagonist means more agonist is required to find free receptors to bind to.

 

In the provided options:

 

  • Curve B, C and D show a lower maximal efficacy at the highest drug concentration, which is not characteristic of a competitive antagonist's effect. Rather these drugs can be non competitive antagonists.

  • Curve E shows a rightward shift with the same maximal efficacy as curve A, which is consistent with the effects of a reversible competitive antagonist.

 

Therefore, the curve that most likely represents the effect of adrenaline after the application of a reversible competitive beta-1 receptor antagonist is Curve E.



ore, the curve that most likely represents the effect of adrenaline after the application of a reversible competitive beta-1 receptor antagonist is Curve E.

Options A. Hypotension caused by Nitroprusside

 

This option is incorrect as hypotension caused by nitroprusside is not typically related to pharmacogenetics. Nitroprusside induces hypotension by releasing nitric oxide, which dilates blood vessels. This effect is predictable and dose-dependent rather than influenced by genetic variability.

 

Options C. Diarrhea caused by physostigmine

 

This option is incorrect. Diarrhea caused by physostigmine is due to its mechanism of action as a cholinesterase inhibitor, increasing acetylcholine levels and stimulating the gastrointestinal tract. This side effect is pharmacodynamic rather than pharmacogenetic.

This option is incorrect because not all the listed conditions are pharmacogenetic. Among the options provided, only hemolytic anemia caused by primaquine is a classic example of a pharmacogenetic condition.

Understand that pharmacogenetic conditions are adverse drug reactions influenced by genetic variations in individuals. Hemolytic anemia due to primaquine in G6PD-deficient individuals is a classic example of a pharmacogenetic condition, unlike hypotension from nitroprusside or diarrhea from physostigmine, which are pharmacodynamic effects.

questions.stemHtml: Identify the type of inhibition from the given graph:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Competitive

 

  • The figure shown in the question is Lineweaver-Burk plot, also known as the double reciprocal plot. 
  • It is constructed by taking the reciprocal of both the reaction velocity (1/V) and the substrate concentration (1/[S]) and plotting them against each other.
  • In this plot, the x-axis represents 1/[S] (the reciprocal of the substrate concentration), and the y-axis represents 1/V (the reciprocal of the reaction velocity). 
  • The slope of the Lineweaver-Burk plot is equal to Km/Vmax, and the intercept on the y-axis is equal to 1/Vmax. 

 

How to interpret this graph?

 

  • X-axis represents Km and Y-axis represents Vmax.
  • If the lines of two graphs (with inhibitor and without inhibitor) intersect at Y-axis, it means Vmax is same and Km is different. This is a case of competitive inhibition.
  • If the lines of two graphs (with inhibitor and without inhibitor) intersect at X-axis, it means Km is same and Vmax is different. This is a case of non-competitive inhibition.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Non-competitive: In non-competitive inhibition, the Vmax decreases (Y-intercept increases), but Km remains the same. This does not match the given graph.

 

Option C. Un-competitive: In uncompetitive inhibition, both Vmax and Km decrease in parallel (lines are parallel on the plot). This is not shown in the graph.

 

Option D. Allosteric: Allosteric inhibition is usually described with sigmoidal (non-Michaelis–Menten) kinetics, not with a straight Lineweaver–Burk plot like this.

 

Educational Objective:

 

In a Lineweaver–Burk plot, competitive inhibition shows unchanged Vmax (same Y-intercept) and increased Km (shift in X-intercept), as seen in the provided graph.

Ans. B) If serum paracetamol levels fall above the treatment line of the Rumack–Matthew nomogram, N-acetylcysteine should be initiated, preferably within 8 hours of ingestion

    • Enhances nontoxic sulfate conjugation,
    • Directly binds NAPQI.

questions.stemHtml: After 15 days of chemotherapy, a patient develops rash and itching on the back as shown in the image. It can occur as a side effect of which of the following drugs?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Bleomycin

 

Bleomycin is a chemotherapeutic agent that is known to cause a distinctive pattern of skin pigmentation called "flagellate pigmentation". This pattern is characterized by linear streaks of hyperpigmentation that resemble the tracks left by a whip, or flagellum. This reaction is more commonly seen in women and can occur several weeks to months after starting therapy. The pigmentation usually resolves spontaneously, but in some cases, it can persist for several months to years after stopping the medication.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Actinomycin: While actinomycin can cause side effects including nausea and myelosuppression, it is not typically associated with flagellate pigmentation.

 

Option B. Doxorubicin: Doxorubicin's side effect profile includes cardiotoxicity and myelosuppression; flagellate pigmentation is not a common reaction with this drug.

 

Option D. Mitomycin C: This chemotherapeutic agent is more commonly associated with bone marrow suppression and renal toxicity, not the distinctive skin pigmentation seen with Bleomycin.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Flagellate pigmentation is a distinctive cutaneous side effect associated with Bleomycin therapy.

questions.stem: The dose of which of the following drugs should be reduced when prescribed along with allopurinol?
questions.solutionHtml:
ibri,sans-serif">Explanation:

 

Option A. Methotrexate: While methotrexate is metabolized by the liver and excreted by the kidneys, allopurinol does not significantly affect its plasma levels. However, close monitoring is still warranted due to the potential for increased toxicity, but specific dose reduction due to allopurinol is not a standard practice.

 

Option C. 6-Thioguanine: Like 6-MP, 6-thioguanine is a purine analog, and though it has a similar mechanism of action, the effect of allopurinol on its metabolism does not usually require a dose adjustment.

 

Option D. Capecitabine: Capecitabine, an oral prodrug that is metabolized into 5-fluorouracil, is not primarily affected by allopurinol, and dose adjustments are typically not necessary when these drugs are used concurrently.

 

Educational Objective:

 

When prescribing 6-Mercaptopurine in conjunction with allopurinol, it's essential to reduce the dosage of 6-MP to prevent increased drug levels and potential toxicity due to the inhibition of xanthine oxidase by allopurinol.

 

This drug interaction underscores the importance of understanding the metabolic pathways of chemotherapeutic agents and the impact of concomitant medications on these pathways.



ore, when allopurinol is administered concurrently with 6-MP, the dose of 6-MP must be reduced (commonly to one-third or one-fourth of its standard dose) to prevent potentially life-threatening toxicity.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements regarding monoclonal antibodies is false?

options.label: A
options.text: Infliximab is a humanized monoclonal antibody, whereas certolizumab is chimeric.

options.label: B
options.text: Trastuzumab targets HER-2 receptors, is used in HER2-positive breast cancer, and can cause cardiotoxicity.

options.label: C
options.text: Eptinezumab is used in prophylaxis of migraine by targeting the CGRP pathway.

options.label: D
options.text: Raxibacumab is effective against anthrax by targeting the protective antigen of Bacillus anthracis.

questions.answerText: Infliximab is a humanized monoclonal antibody, whereas certolizumab is chimeric.
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Infliximab is a humanized monoclonal antibody, whereas certolizumab is chimeric.

 

Infliximab is actually a chimeric monoclonal antibody (suffix -ximab) against TNF-α. Certolizumab, on the other hand, is a humanized PEGylated Fab fragment against TNF-α. So the statement is wrong.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Trastuzumab targets HER-2 receptors, is used in HER2-positive breast cancer, and can cause cardiotoxicity: True.Trastuzumab is a humanized monoclonal antibody (suffix -zumab) against HER2/neu (ErbB2) receptor. Used in HER2-positive breast cancer & gastric cancer. Adverse effect: cardiotoxicity (dilated cardiomyopathy).

 

Option C. Eptinezumab is used in prophylaxis of migraine by targeting the CGRP pathway: True.Eptinezumab is a monoclonal antibody against CGRP used in migraine prophylaxis. Other members: erenumab (CGRP receptor), fremanezumab, galcanezumab.

 

Option D. Raxibacumab is effective against anthrax by targeting the protective antigen of Bacillus anthracis: True.Raxibacumab is a human monoclonal antibody against the protective antigen of Bacillus anthracis. Used for treatment and prophylaxis of inhalational anthrax.
